questions.body: What are the two fundamental 'Rules of Hooks' in React?
questions.keyPoints: Only call hooks at the top level (never in loops, conditions, or nested functions), and only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.

options.text: 1. Only call hooks at the top level (not inside loops, conditions, or nested functions). 2. Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.
options.explanation: React relies on the call order of hooks remaining identical between renders to map each hook's state to its corresponding internal fiber node.

options.text: 1. Only call hooks inside `try...catch` blocks. 2. Always pass a key prop to hooks.
options.explanation: Calling hooks inside blocks breaks render call order consistency.

options.text: 1. Hooks must return promises. 2. Hooks can only be called from class components.
options.explanation: Hooks cannot be used in class components at all.

options.text: 1. Hooks must be registered in `package.json`. 2. Never call more than 5 hooks per component.
options.explanation: There is no arbitrary count limit, and hooks are standard JavaScript functions.

questions.body: In React 18, how does automatic state batching handle multiple state updates triggered inside setTimeout, promises, or native event handlers?
questions.keyPoints: React 18 batches all state updates automatically into a single re-render, regardless of origin.

options.text: All state updates are automatically batched into a single re-render, regardless of whether they originate from React events, promises, `setTimeout`, or native events.
options.explanation: React 18 introduced Automatic Batching across all contexts out-of-the-box. Prior to React 18, only updates inside React synthetic event handlers were batched automatically.

options.text: Updates inside `setTimeout` are never batched and always trigger individual re-renders.
options.explanation: That was the behavior in React 17 and earlier; React 18 batches them.

options.text: Batching only applies if the component is wrapped in `React.memo`.
options.explanation: Automatic batching is a core reconciler feature across all components.

options.text: State batching requires calling `ReactDOM.flushSync()` explicitly.
options.explanation: `flushSync` is used to OPT OUT of automatic batching when immediate DOM reads are required.

questions.keyPoints: All three calls reference the stale count value (0) from the current render closure, resulting in 1.

options.explanation: Because `count` is captured from the current render's closure (`0`), each call executes `setCount(0 + 1)`. To increment to 3, the updater function `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` must be used.
`3` would only occur with functional updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)`.
The state updates to 1 upon re-render.

options.text: `NaN`
options.explanation: `0 + 1` produces number 1.

questions.body: When does the cleanup function returned from a `useEffect` callback run?
questions.keyPoints: Runs before the effect re-runs on dependency change, and when the component unmounts.

options.text: Before the effect re-runs due to a dependency change, and immediately before the component unmounts from the DOM.
options.explanation: The cleanup function cleans up resources from the PREVIOUS render before the effect executes for the NEW render, and cleans up completely on unmount.

options.text: Only once when the component unmounts.
options.explanation: It also executes before every re-execution of the effect.

options.text: Synchronously during the initial render phase.
options.explanation: Effects and cleanups execute after layout and paint in the commit phase.

options.text: Whenever any child component re-renders.
options.explanation: It depends strictly on the effect's own dependency array.

questions.body: What is the critical timing difference between `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect`?
questions.keyPoints: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but before the browser paints; useEffect fires asynchronously after paint.

options.text: `useLayoutEffect` fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but BEFORE the browser paints; `useEffect` runs asynchronously AFTER the browser has painted to the screen.
options.explanation: `useLayoutEffect` blocks painting, making it ideal for measuring DOM layout (e.g. tooltip dimensions) and immediately updating state to avoid visual flickering. `useEffect` is non-blocking.

options.text: `useEffect` runs on the server; `useLayoutEffect` runs on the client.
options.explanation: `useLayoutEffect` outputs a warning on the server because the server has no layout engine.

options.text: `useLayoutEffect` is only used for CSS transitions.
options.explanation: It is used for synchronous DOM measurement and mutation.

options.text: `useEffect` cannot access DOM references via `ref`.
options.explanation: Both hooks can access DOM refs since both run in or after the commit phase.

questions.body: What does `useCallback(fn, deps)` return?
questions.keyPoints: Returns a memoized version of the callback function that only changes if dependencies change.

options.text: A memoized version of the callback function instance that retains referential equality across renders unless its dependencies change.
options.explanation: `useCallback` returns the exact same function reference between renders if dependencies haven't changed, preventing unnecessary re-renders of memoized child components (`React.memo`) that receive the callback as a prop.

options.text: The evaluated return value of the function `fn`.
options.explanation: `useMemo` returns the evaluated result of a function; `useCallback` returns the function definition itself.

options.text: A promise that resolves when the callback finishes executing.
options.explanation: It returns a standard synchronous function.

options.text: A debounced version of the function.
options.explanation: It does not debounce or throttle.

questions.body: What is the relationship between `useCallback` and `useMemo` in React?
questions.keyPoints: useCallback(fn, deps) is syntactically equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps).

options.text: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.
options.explanation: `useCallback` is syntactic sugar around `useMemo` specifically tailored for caching function references rather than arbitrary computed values.

options.text: `useCallback` can only be used with asynchronous functions.
options.explanation: Both work on synchronous and asynchronous functions.

options.text: `useMemo` caches values across different browser tabs via localStorage.
options.explanation: It only caches values in memory for the component instance lifecycle.

options.text: `useCallback` runs during the commit phase, while `useMemo` runs during paint.
options.explanation: Both execute during the render phase.

questions.body: Does mutating the `ref.current` property of a `useRef` object trigger a component re-render?
questions.keyPoints: No, mutating ref.current does not trigger a re-render.

options.text: No, mutating `.current` is a silent in-memory mutation that does NOT cause a re-render.
options.explanation: `useRef` returns a plain mutable object `{ current: initialValue }` that persists across renders. Modifying `.current` never triggers a re-render.

options.text: Yes, it triggers an immediate synchronous re-render like `useState`.
options.explanation: Only state setters (`setState` / `dispatch`) trigger re-renders.

options.text: Yes, but only in development mode.
options.explanation: It never triggers a re-render in either mode.

options.text: Only if `ref.current` is set to null.
options.explanation: The value assigned does not affect re-render behavior.

questions.body: When is `useReducer` generally preferred over multiple `useState` calls?
questions.keyPoints: When state logic is complex, involves multiple sub-values, or next state depends on previous state in intricate ways.

options.text: When managing complex state logic involving multiple related sub-values, or when the next state depends intricately on previous state and distinct action types.
options.explanation: `useReducer` consolidates state transition logic into a pure reducer function `(state, action) => newState`, separating state transitions from component rendering and simplifying testing.

options.text: When you want to share state globally across unrelated components without Context.
options.explanation: `useReducer` is local to the component instance unless paired with Context.

options.text: When managing primitive boolean or string values.
options.explanation: `useState` is simpler and more concise for independent primitive values.

options.text: Because `useReducer` runs on a Web Worker thread.
options.explanation: Both hooks run in the standard React reconciler.

questions.body: What is the primary naming convention for Custom Hooks in React, and why is it enforced by ESLint?
questions.keyPoints: Must start with 'use' (e.g. useDebounce); allows linter to enforce the Rules of Hooks.

options.text: They must start with the prefix `use` (e.g., `useWindowSize`), allowing React and the ESLint plugin to identify them and enforce the Rules of Hooks.
options.explanation: The `use` prefix is an explicit convention that tells the React linter that this function may contain calls to other hooks, ensuring the Rules of Hooks are checked.

options.text: They must end with `Hook` (e.g., `windowSizeHook`).
options.explanation: The prefix must be `use`.

options.text: They must be written in PascalCase like components (e.g., `WindowSize`).
options.explanation: Components use PascalCase; custom hooks use camelCase starting with `use`.

options.text: They must be registered in the global React namespace.
options.explanation: They are standard modular JavaScript functions.

questions.body: What does the `useTransition` hook in React 18 enable?
questions.keyPoints: Marks state updates as non-urgent transitions, keeping the UI responsive to user input.

options.text: It lets you mark state updates as non-urgent transitions, allowing urgent updates (like typing in an input) to interrupt the render and keep the UI responsive.
options.explanation: `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();` allows slow or heavy rendering updates (like filtering a 10,000 item list) to be interrupted by user keystrokes, avoiding input lag.

options.text: It automatically generates CSS keyframe animations for page transitions.
options.explanation: It manages React rendering priority, not CSS animations.

options.text: It converts synchronous code to run inside a Web Worker thread.
options.explanation: Concurrent rendering runs on the main thread via task slicing.

options.text: It replaces `useNavigate` in React Router.
options.explanation: It is a core React priority management hook.

questions.body: How does `useDeferredValue(value)` differ from debouncing with `setTimeout`?
questions.keyPoints: useDeferredValue is deeply integrated with React's concurrent scheduler; it defers rendering only while urgent updates occur, with no fixed artificial delay.

options.text: It adapts to the user's device speed and starts rendering the deferred value as soon as urgent work completes, without any artificial fixed millisecond delay.
options.explanation: Unlike debouncing (which imposes a fixed delay like 300ms even on fast machines), `useDeferredValue` adapts dynamically: on fast devices the update appears almost instantly; on slow devices it yields to keystrokes.

options.text: It cancels previous HTTP fetch requests automatically.
options.explanation: It defers React rendering, not network fetches.

options.text: It stores previous values in `sessionStorage`.
options.explanation: It is purely in-memory concurrent state.

options.text: It delays updates by a mandatory minimum of 1000 milliseconds.
options.explanation: There is no fixed time delay.

questions.body: Why was the `useId` hook introduced in React 18?
questions.keyPoints: Generates unique, stable IDs across client and server to prevent hydration mismatch errors in accessibility labels.

options.text: To generate unique, stable IDs that match between server-rendered HTML and client hydration, specifically for connecting accessibility attributes (`htmlFor`, `aria-describedby`).
options.explanation: Random number generators like `Math.random()` cause hydration mismatches between SSR HTML and the client. `useId()` produces deterministic, collision-free IDs based on component tree position.

options.text: To generate database primary keys for GraphQL mutations.
options.explanation: It is purely for DOM accessibility element associations.

options.text: To provide unique keys for array mapping automatically.
options.explanation: The React documentation explicitly cautions against using `useId` to generate array list keys.

options.text: To identify user authentication sessions in cookies.
options.explanation: It generates DOM element identifiers.

questions.body: Why was `useSyncExternalStore` added to React 18 for third-party state libraries (Redux, Zustand)?
questions.keyPoints: To prevent 'tearing' (visual inconsistency where components render with different versions of external store data) during concurrent rendering.

options.text: To safely subscribe to external stores without 'tearing' (inconsistent UI where different components render with different versions of the store during concurrent renders).
options.explanation: During concurrent rendering, React can pause work. If an external store mutates in between, different components might read different values. `useSyncExternalStore` forces synchronous reads to eliminate tearing.

options.text: To synchronize data directly with PostgreSQL databases via WebSockets.
options.explanation: External store means state managers outside React (e.g. Redux, browser history).

options.text: To replace the browser `localStorage` API.
options.explanation: It is a React hook for library authors.

options.text: To automatically encrypt state payloads.
options.explanation: It guarantees synchronous data consistency during concurrent rendering.

questions.body: When used alongside `forwardRef`, what does `useImperativeHandle(ref, createHandle, [deps])` accomplish?
questions.keyPoints: Customizes the instance value exposed to parent components when using ref.

options.text: It customizes and limits the imperative handle methods exposed to parent components via a `ref`, rather than exposing the raw underlying DOM node.
options.explanation: Instead of leaking an entire raw `<input>` DOM node to a parent, `useImperativeHandle` allows the child to expose only specific methods like `focus()` or `scrollIntoView()`.

options.text: It binds Redux actions directly to DOM elements.
options.explanation: It has no relation to Redux.

options.text: It forces synchronous paint operations on the child component.
options.explanation: It shapes the object exposed on the forwarded ref.

options.text: It allows class components to call functional hooks.
options.explanation: It is a functional hook used with `forwardRef`.

questions.keyPoints: The interval callback closes over the initial render's count variable and never sees subsequent state updates.

options.text: The effect callback runs only once on mount, closing over the initial `count` value (`0`); the interval callback continues logging that stale initial closure variable forever.
options.explanation: Because `count` is omitted from dependencies, the effect never re-synchronizes when `count` updates, causing the callback to retain the captured initial state value.

options.text: JavaScript Garbage Collection destroys the `count` variable after 5 seconds.
options.explanation: The variable stays alive in memory precisely because the closure holds a reference to it.

options.text: `setInterval` is forbidden inside React components.
options.explanation: `setInterval` is standard web API usage in effects.

options.text: The timer automatically resets to 0 on every tick.
options.explanation: The issue is lexical closure scoping in JavaScript.

questions.body: How can you prevent an expensive computation from executing on every render when initializing state with `useState`?
questions.keyPoints: Pass a function to useState: useState(() => computeExpensiveValue()).

options.text: Pass a function to `useState`: `useState(() => computeExpensiveValue())` (lazy initial state).
options.explanation: If you write `useState(expensive())`, the function executes on every render even though its return value is only used on initial mount. Passing `useState(() => expensive())` ensures it runs only once on mount.

options.text: Wrap the initial value in `Object.freeze()`.
options.explanation: `Object.freeze` prevents property mutations, but does not prevent computation on re-renders.

options.text: Use `useRef` inside the `useState` call.
options.explanation: Hooks cannot be nested inside hook calls.

options.text: State initialization can never be optimized in React.
options.explanation: Lazy initialization is the documented, standard React pattern for this.

questions.body: When a Context Provider's `value` changes, what happens to child components that consume that context with `useContext`?
questions.keyPoints: All consuming components re-render, even if wrapped in React.memo.

options.text: Every component that consumes that context will re-render, bypassing any `React.memo` optimizations on those consuming components.
options.explanation: When context value changes, every component calling `useContext(MyContext)` re-renders automatically. `React.memo` only bails out when props change; it does not block context updates.

options.text: Only components with changed props re-render.
options.explanation: Context changes trigger re-renders of all consumers regardless of props.

options.text: `React.memo` prevents the consuming component from updating.
options.explanation: React explicitly forces context consumers to re-render.

options.text: Context updates are batched until browser restart.
options.explanation: Context updates re-render consumers immediately within the current render cycle.

questions.body: If two different components call the exact same custom hook `useCounter()`, do they share the same state?
questions.keyPoints: No, each call to a custom hook creates completely isolated independent state.

options.text: No, each invocation of a custom hook creates completely independent, isolated state and effects.
options.explanation: Custom hooks are a mechanism for reusing stateful logic (code), not state itself. Each component calling a custom hook gets its own isolated instance of the hook's internal state.

options.text: Yes, custom hooks act as global singleton state managers automatically.
options.explanation: To share state globally, custom hooks must be combined with Context or an external store.

options.text: They share state only if they have the same parent component.
options.explanation: Hook state is strictly bound to the specific component instance that invoked it.

options.text: Calling a custom hook twice throws an exception.
options.explanation: Custom hooks can be called across as many components as needed.

questions.body: What is the specialized purpose of the `useInsertionEffect` hook introduced in React 18?
questions.keyPoints: Fires before all DOM mutations; intended exclusively for CSS-in-JS libraries injecting dynamic style tags.

options.text: It fires synchronously BEFORE all DOM mutations, intended exclusively for CSS-in-JS libraries (like styled-components) to inject `<style>` tags before reading layout.
options.explanation: `useInsertionEffect` is a specialized hook designed for CSS-in-JS authors to inject styles into the DOM before `useLayoutEffect` runs, preventing expensive style recalculations and layout thrashing.

options.text: It inserts raw HTML without sanitization.
options.explanation: It has nothing to do with innerHTML injection.

options.text: It inserts database records into IndexedDB.
options.explanation: It is a React lifecycle hook for style injection.

options.text: It replaces `useCallback` for event handlers.
options.explanation: It is strictly a CSS-in-JS timing mechanism.
